sketches.title: Laundry Legend
sketches.premise: Both players turn the same ordinary chore into a motivational-poster headline. Make folding laundry sound heroic, tender, or gloriously overdramatic; the Judge rewards the headline that travels furthest without losing the chore.
sketches.criterion: The headline must still clearly motivate someone to do the named chore.
sketches.move_shape: Write one poster headline of up to 160 characters for the chore card, using its two prompt nouns; for “fold socks / lost pair,” write: “FOLD SOCKS: reunite the tiny travelers before they start a new family.”

sketches.title: Scrub Story
sketches.premise: A chore card gives you a plain task and two nouns hiding in it. Write one tiny motivational poster line that makes the task feel like a quest, while keeping both nouns honestly on the poster; the Judge rewards the biggest leap from drudgery to destiny.
sketches.criterion: The line must still describe or urge the exact chore and must include both given nouns in a meaningful way.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence or headline of up to 160 characters; for “take out trash / bag,” write: “TAKE OUT THE TRASH: carry the brave bag beyond the gate and let tomorrow breathe.”

sketches.title: Heroic Housework
sketches.premise: You and the House receive the same chore and two everyday nouns. Turn them into a motivational-poster caption, but do not dodge the chore with a joke or a story; the more inspiring the climb while the chore stays visible, the more points you earn.
sketches.criterion: The answer must contain a recognizable call to do the dealt chore, with both nouns used as part of that call.
sketches.move_shape: Write one poster caption of up to 160 characters; for “sweep floor / crumbs,” write: “SWEEP THE FLOOR: send every crumb marching toward its quiet little freedom.”

sketches.title: Clean Queen
sketches.premise: The House deals a chore with two nouns, and both players crown it with a motivational-poster headline. Keep the chore and both nouns in view, then make the line as grand, sweet, or cheeky as you like; bland obedience earns a polite royal nod and almost no points.
sketches.criterion: The headline must urge the named chore and preserve a clear, fair role for both prompt nouns.
sketches.move_shape: Write one headline of up to 160 characters; for “dust shelf / book,” write: “DUST THE SHELF: clear the way so every book can stand tall and show off.”

sketches.title: Tiny Task Triumph
sketches.premise: Both players answer one chore card with a poster slogan built from its two nouns. The Judge checks whether it remains a real reason to do that chore, then pays for imagination, warmth, and a little sparkle; yes, even your mop gets a character arc.
sketches.criterion: The slogan must remain a genuine motivational reason to complete the exact chore while using both nouns.
sketches.move_shape: Write one slogan of up to 160 characters; for “water plant / cup,” write: “WATER THE PLANT: one small cup, one brave thirst, one green victory by breakfast.”

sketches.title: Poster of Purpose
sketches.premise: A chore arrives with two plain nouns, and you make a motivational poster for it. Your line may be heartfelt, absurd, or lightly teasing, but it must leave no doubt what chore a tired stranger should do; the farther it rises above the obvious, the better.
sketches.criterion: The answer must plainly motivate the dealt chore and give both nouns a meaningful place without changing the task.
sketches.move_shape: Write one poster line of up to 160 characters; for “hang coat / hook,” write: “HANG THE COAT: give the hook its purpose and your tomorrow-self a softer landing.”
